name: Apoliticism
scope: Apoliticism as a stance toward politics: being uninterested or uninvolved in it, or averse to it (Merriam-Webster, 'having no interest in or involvement in political affairs … having an aversion to politics'), or claiming political neutrality (Collins, 'politically neutral; without political attitudes, content, or bias'). The scholarship that names it applies it to the Epicurean advice to stay out of public life (Grosz: 'Epicurus' unapologetically apolitical stance'; Edinburgh thesis on Roman Epicureans' professed quietude) and distinguishes it from antipolitical rejection of existing politics (Nietzsche as 'antipolitisch', not 'unpolitisch'). It excludes partisan centrism and organised abstention movements, and the Anabaptist separation from the state, which no source here ties to the name. Epicurus himself is Epicureanism's namesake, so he is no key figure here.

summary: Apoliticism is a stance of being uninterested or uninvolved in politics, averse to it, or claiming political neutrality. The scholarship that names it applies it chiefly to Epicurus' reasoned teaching of withdrawal from public life and to the professed quietude of Roman Epicureans. It is a stance about participation, not a programme, so it settles almost no policy question.
notes: Only one statement (withdraw-from-politics) is settled by the defining sources; the dictionaries define the word without taking policy positions, so every other statement is null. The Anabaptist strand is out of scope because no source here ties it to the name.
